title: P3 Motion
subtitle: Speed, graph skills, distance–time graphs, acceleration and speed–time graphs
lede: Everything on the P3 revision checklist, in order. Each lesson's ideas are explained, shown in a worked example, then practised straight away — with answers checked as you go.
howto: Read the explanation. Cover it up and try to say it back to yourself in your own words.
Study the worked example. Reveal the steps one at a time and notice how the answer is laid out, not just what it is.
Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Write every calculation in EWAU layout on paper first, then type the answer to check it.
If you got something wrong, go back to the explanation, then try the question again.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

sections.title: Speed
sections.blurb: What speed means, the speed equation and its rearrangements, laying out calculations with EWAU, and the difference between instantaneous and average speed.
checklist: Know what is meant by the term 'speed'
Calculate the speed of an object
Rearrange the speed equation to calculate distance or time
Use EWAU to lay out calculations
Understand the difference between instantaneous speed and average speed
Know how to calculate average speed

parts.title: What is speed?
parts.html:
Speed tells you how far an object travels every second (or every hour). A faster object covers more distance in the same time.

The equation is:

$$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$$

The units must match up:

Distance in…Time in…Speed in…
metres (m)seconds (s)metres per second (m/s)
kilometres (km)hours (h)kilometres per hour (km/h)
mileshours (h)miles per hour (mph)

In physics we normally use m/s. If a question gives you minutes or kilometres, convert first: 1 minute = 60 s and 1 km = 1000 m.

parts.title: EWAU — how to lay out every calculation
parts.html:
Every calculation in physics should be written out in four lines. This earns marks even if you make a slip with the arithmetic, and it makes your working easy to check.

LetterWhat you write
EquationThe equation in words or symbols, before you put any numbers in.
WorkingThe numbers substituted into the equation.
AnswerThe number you get out.
UnitsThe correct unit written after the answer.

Every worked example and walkthrough on this page is written in EWAU. Copy the layout.

parts.title: Calculating speed
parts.question: A cyclist travels 240 m in 30 s. Calculate her speed.
steps: Check it makes sense: 8 m every second for 30 seconds is $8 \times 30 = 240$ m. ✓

parts.title: Rearranging the speed equation
parts.html:
Sometimes you are given the speed and need to find the distance or the time. Here are all three versions of the equation — learn them:

To find…Use…Why it works
speed$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$This is the original equation.
distance$\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}$Distance was being divided by time, so multiply both sides by time to undo it.
time$\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$Swap speed and time — they are both "underneath" the distance.

Quick check: if you are finding a distance, you multiply. If you are finding a speed or a time, you always divide the distance by something.

questions.hint: The distance is already in km and the time in hours, so no conversion is needed.

parts.title: Instantaneous speed vs average speed
parts.html:
Real journeys are not at one steady speed — you speed up, slow down and stop. So there are two kinds of speed:

TypeMeaningExample
Instantaneous speedThe speed at one particular moment.The reading on a car's speedometer right now; a speed-camera reading.
Average speedThe total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey — including any stops."The coach averaged 60 km/h on the motorway."
$$\text{average speed} = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$$

Common mistake: leaving out the time spent stopped. If you stop for lunch, that time still counts in the total time — it lowers your average speed.

parts.title: Average speed
parts.question: A cyclist rides 1200 m in 100 s, stops for 50 s at a junction, then rides a further 600 m in 50 s. Calculate her average speed for the whole journey.
steps: Add up the totals first. Total distance $= 1200 + 600 = 1800$ m.
Total time $= 100 + 50 + 50 = 200$ s — the 50 s stop counts.
Notice: during the first part her speed was $1200 \div 100 = 12$ m/s, and at the junction it was 0 m/s. The average, 9 m/s, is in between.

questions.text: In your own words, explain the difference between instantaneous speed and average speed.
questions.model: Instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment in time (for example, a speedometer reading). Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time for a whole journey, including any stops.

questions.text: A car travels 30 km in 0.5 h and then 60 km in 1 h. Calculate its average speed in km/h.
questions.hint: Add up the total distance and the total time before you divide.
walkthrough: Total distance $= 30 + 60 = 90$ km. Total time $= 0.5 + 1 = 1.5$ h.

questions.text: An athlete runs 100 m in 12 s, rests for 18 s, then runs another 100 m in 10 s. Calculate her average speed over the whole 40 s.
questions.hint: The rest counts in the total time. Total distance is 200 m.
walkthrough: Total distance $= 100 + 100 = 200$ m. Total time $= 12 + 18 + 10 = 40$ s.

questions.text: A speedometer in a car reads 70 mph. Is this an instantaneous speed or an average speed?
questions.explain: A speedometer shows the speed at that exact moment, not over a whole journey — so it is an instantaneous speed.

questions.text: A cyclist's average speed over 300 s is 6 m/s.

parts.text: Calculate the distance he travelled.
parts.hint: Rearrange: distance = speed × time.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Does this mean he was travelling at 6 m/s the whole time? Explain your answer.
parts.model: No. An average speed only tells you the overall speed for the whole journey. He could have gone faster at some times and slower (or stopped) at others.
parts.label: b

sections.title: Graph skills
sections.blurb: Line graphs and scatter graphs, when to draw a line of best fit and when to join dot-to-dot, drawing graphs correctly, and calculating a gradient.
checklist: Understand the difference between line and scatter graphs
Understand when to draw a line of best fit and when to connect points dot-to-dot
Correctly draw line and scatter graphs
Calculate the gradient of a line
Understand that a gradient can be positive or negative and what this tells you about the slope

parts.title: Line graphs vs scatter graphs
parts.html:
Both graphs plot one number against another, but they are used for different jobs.

Line graphScatter graph
When you use itYou chose the values of the variable on the x-axis (the independent variable) and measured what happened to the other one.You measured both variables and want to see if there is a correlation (a link) between them.
ExampleDistance travelled every 10 s; extension of a spring for different forces; temperature of water each minute.Height vs arm span of 30 pupils; hours of sleep vs test score.
The linePoints are joined — either with a line of best fit or dot-to-dot (see below).Points are not joined dot-to-dot. A line of best fit can be added if there is a clear correlation.

parts.title: Line of best fit or dot-to-dot?
parts.html:
Draw a…When…How
Line of best fitYou expect a smooth pattern and the points are slightly scattered because of small measurement errors. Most science experiments are like this.One straight line (ruler!) or one smooth curve that passes through the middle of the points, with roughly as many above as below. Ignore anomalous points (ones clearly off the pattern) and circle them.
Dot-to-dotThere is no reason to expect a smooth pattern between readings — the thing being measured can change suddenly. Journey graphs (distance–time and speed–time) are usually drawn like this, because a car can stop at lights or suddenly accelerate.Join each point to the next with a straight ruled line.

parts.title: Drawing a graph correctly — the checklist
parts.html:
1. Axes: independent variable (the one you changed or chose, usually time) on the x-axis; dependent variable (the one you measured) on the y-axis.
  2. Labels: each axis labelled with the quantity and its unit, e.g. "Distance (m)".
  3. Scale: goes up in equal steps (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50…) and the plotted points fill more than half of the grid in both directions.
  4. Plot: small, neat crosses (×) with a sharp pencil.
  5. Line: best fit (ruler or smooth curve) or dot-to-dot — decide which before you draw.
  6. Title if asked, e.g. "Distance–time graph for a cyclist".

parts.title: Gradient
parts.html:
The gradient is a number that tells you how steep a line is. It is "how much the line goes up for every 1 it goes across":

$$\text{gradient} = \dfrac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x} = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$$

Method:

  1. Choose two points on the line, as far apart as possible (big triangles give more accurate answers).
  2. Draw a right-angled triangle between them.
  3. Read off the change in $y$ (the vertical side) and the change in $x$ (the horizontal side).
  4. Divide: change in $y$ ÷ change in $x$.

Positive or negative?

  • A line that slopes up to the right has a positive gradient — $y$ gets bigger as $x$ gets bigger.
  • A line that slopes down to the right has a negative gradient — $y$ gets smaller as $x$ gets bigger.
  • A horizontal line has a gradient of zero — $y$ doesn't change at all.
  • The bigger the number (ignoring the sign), the steeper the line.

parts.title: Finding a gradient
parts.question: Find the gradient of the line shown.

graph.alt: A straight line through the origin, with a triangle drawn between (2, 10) and (8, 40)

steps: Choose two points on the line, far apart: $(2,\ 10)$ and $(8,\ 40)$.
The gradient is $+5$: the line goes up 5 for every 1 it goes across.
A line from $(0,\ 20)$ to $(10,\ 0)$ would have gradient $\dfrac{0 - 20}{10 - 0} = \dfrac{-20}{10} = -2$ — negative, because it slopes downwards.

sections.title: Distance–time graphs
sections.blurb: Reading the shape of a distance–time graph, finding the speed from its gradient, and drawing one from a description of a journey.
checklist: Know how constant speed, stationary, constant speed towards home, speeding up and slowing down are shown on a distance–time graph
Use the gradient to work out the speed from a distance–time graph
Draw a distance–time graph to represent a journey

parts.title: Reading a distance–time graph
parts.html:
A distance–time graph has distance from the start on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. The shape of the line tells you what the object is doing:

Shape of lineWhat the object is doing
Straight line sloping upwardsConstant speed, moving away from the start. The steeper the line, the faster it is going.
Horizontal lineStationary (not moving). Distance stays the same as time passes.
Straight line sloping downwardsConstant speed back towards the start (heading home). The distance from the start is getting smaller.
Curve getting steeperSpeeding up (accelerating) — covering more distance each second.
Curve getting flatterSlowing down (decelerating) — covering less distance each second.

graph.alt: The five shapes on a distance–time graph: rising line, flat line, falling line, curve getting steeper, curve getting flatter

parts.after:
The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed. That is because gradient $= \dfrac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x} = \dfrac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}$ — which is exactly the speed equation.

A negative gradient just means the object is moving back towards the start. Its speed is still a positive number (the size of the gradient).

parts.title: Finding speeds from a distance–time graph
parts.question: The graph shows a pupil walking to a post box and back. Describe each stage and find the speed in each.

graph.alt: Distance–time graph: up to 100 m in 20 s, flat for 20 s, back to 0 in 20 s

steps: A (0–20 s): straight sloping line — constant speed away from home.
C (40–60 s): straight line sloping down — constant speed back towards home.
Speed in B: the line is horizontal, so the gradient is 0 and the speed is 0 m/s.
Speed in C — between $(40,\ 100)$ and $(60,\ 0)$: gradient $= \dfrac{0 - 100}{60 - 40} = \dfrac{-100}{20} = -5$. The gradient is negative because she is heading home; her speed is 5 m/s.

parts.title: Drawing a distance–time graph for a journey
parts.html:
1. Read the journey carefully and split it into stages. Write down the time at the end of each stage (add the times up as you go) and the distance from the start at that moment.
  2. Plot each of these as a point.
  3. Join the points dot-to-dot with a ruler (a journey can change suddenly, so no line of best fit).
  4. Check: stationary stages must be horizontal; returning home must slope back down to zero.

sections.title: Acceleration
sections.blurb: What acceleration means, calculating it (including deceleration), and planning a practical to measure it with good measurements.
checklist: Know what is meant by the term 'acceleration'
Calculate the size of the acceleration of an object
Devise a practical to measure the acceleration of an object
Take appropriate measurements in a practical

parts.title: What is acceleration?
parts.html:
Acceleration is how quickly the speed changes — the change in speed every second.

$$\text{acceleration} = \dfrac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{time taken}} = \dfrac{\text{final speed} - \text{initial speed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

Using symbols, where $u$ is the initial (starting) speed and $v$ is the final speed:

$$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$$

Units: speed is in m/s and time is in s, so acceleration is in (m/s) per s, written m/s² ("metres per second squared"). An acceleration of 3 m/s² means the speed increases by 3 m/s every second.

  • If the object is speeding up, the acceleration is positive.
  • If the object is slowing down, the acceleration is negative. This is called a deceleration.
  • "From rest" or "starts from stationary" means $u = 0$. "Comes to a stop" means $v = 0$.

parts.title: Calculating acceleration
parts.question: A car accelerates from rest to 24 m/s in 8 s. Calculate its acceleration.
steps: From rest means the initial speed $u = 0$ m/s. Final speed $v = 24$ m/s. Time $t = 8$ s.

parts.title: Deceleration
parts.question: A cyclist slows from 10 m/s to 4 m/s in 3 s. Calculate her acceleration.
steps: The minus sign shows she is slowing down: a deceleration of 2 m/s².

questions.text: Acceleration is the change in … every second.
questions.explain: Acceleration is the change in speed every second. Its unit is m/s².

questions.text: A train starts from rest and reaches 30 m/s after 60 s. Calculate its acceleration.
A ball speeds up from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in 4 s. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.hint: Final speed minus initial speed, divided by the time.

questions.text: A car brakes from 20 m/s to 5 m/s in 5 s. Calculate its acceleration. (Include the sign.)
questions.hint: It is slowing down, so expect a negative answer.
walkthrough: The negative sign shows the car is slowing down — a deceleration of 3 m/s².

questions.text: A rocket sled accelerates from rest at 2 m/s² for 6 s. What is its final speed?
questions.hint: Rearrange: change in speed = acceleration × time. It started from rest.
walkthrough: It started from rest, so final speed $= 0 + 12 = 12$ m/s.

questions.text: Explain why the unit of acceleration is m/s² and not m/s.
questions.model: Acceleration is a change in speed (m/s) divided by a time (s). (m/s) ÷ s = m/s². It tells you how many m/s the speed changes by each second, which is a different kind of quantity from a speed.

parts.title: Devising a practical to measure acceleration
parts.html:
To find an acceleration you need to measure two things: the change in speed and the time it took. Here is a method for a trolley rolling down a ramp.

Equipment

Trolley, ramp, two light gates connected to a timer/datalogger, a card of known length fixed to the trolley, a ruler, a stopwatch (as a back-up).

Method

  1. Measure the length of the card with a ruler (in metres).
  2. Release the trolley from the same mark on the ramp each time (don't push it).
  3. Each light gate records how long the card takes to pass through it. Speed at a gate $= \dfrac{\text{card length}}{\text{time to pass through}}$. This gives $u$ at gate 1 and $v$ at gate 2.
  4. The timer also records the time taken to travel from gate 1 to gate 2. This is $t$.
  5. Calculate $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$.
  6. Repeat at least three times and calculate a mean. Ignore any anomalous result.

Why light gates and not a stopwatch?

A person's reaction time (about 0.2 s) makes stopwatch timings unreliable when the times are short. Light gates start and stop automatically, so the measurement is more accurate.

Variables

TypeIn this experiment
Independent (the one you change)e.g. the height (steepness) of the ramp, if you are investigating what affects the acceleration.
Dependent (the one you measure)The acceleration of the trolley (found from the speeds and time).
Control (kept the same)Same trolley, same mass, same release point, same distance between the light gates, same surface.

Taking good measurements

  • Use the right instrument: ruler for the card length, light gates for short times.
  • Read scales at eye level to avoid parallax error.
  • Record results in a table with headings and units, and repeat to spot anomalies.
  • Write times to a sensible number of decimal places (what the timer actually shows).

questions.text: A pupil wants to measure the acceleration of a toy car rolling down a slope. Describe a method she could use. Include: the equipment, what she would measure, how she would calculate the acceleration, and one way to make the results more reliable.
questions.model: A good answer includes: equipment (slope, toy car, two light gates and timer — or a stopwatch — ruler, card); measuring the card length with a ruler; measuring the speed at two points (card length ÷ time through each light gate); measuring the time between the two points; calculating $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$; releasing from the same point without pushing; repeating at least three times and finding a mean, discarding anomalies; keeping the slope angle and car the same.

parts.hint: Speed = card length ÷ time to pass through.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the speed at gate 2.
parts.hint: Same card, shorter time — so a faster speed.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.
parts.hint: u is the speed at gate 1, v the speed at gate 2, t the time between them.

questions.text: Explain why using a stopwatch to time the card through a light gate's position would give a less accurate result than using the light gate itself.
questions.model: The time for a card to pass through a gate is very short (a fraction of a second). Human reaction time (about 0.2 s) is a large fraction of that, so the stopwatch reading would be far too inaccurate. A light gate starts and stops the timer automatically.

questions.text: A pupil's three repeat readings for the time between gates are 0.61 s, 0.59 s and 0.92 s. Which reading is anomalous, and what should the pupil do about it?
questions.model: 0.92 s is anomalous — it is much larger than the other two. The pupil should ignore it when calculating the mean (and repeat the reading if possible). Mean of the other two $= \dfrac{0.61 + 0.59}{2} = 0.60$ s.

parts.title: Watch out!
parts.html: A speed–time graph looks similar to a distance–time graph but means something completely different. Always read the y-axis label first. A horizontal line on a distance–time graph means stationary; a horizontal line on a speed–time graph means constant speed.

parts.title: Reading a speed–time graph
parts.html:
A speed–time graph has speed on the y-axis and time on the x-axis.

Shape of lineWhat the object is doing
Horizontal line above the x-axisConstant speed. Speed is not changing.
Horizontal line along the x-axis (speed = 0)Stationary.
Straight line sloping upwardsConstant acceleration — speeding up steadily. Steeper = bigger acceleration.
Straight line sloping downwardsConstant deceleration — slowing down steadily.

graph.alt: The shapes on a speed–time graph: rising line, flat line, falling line, line along the axis

parts.after: The gradient of a speed–time graph is the acceleration, because gradient $= \dfrac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{change in time}}$, which is the acceleration equation. A negative gradient is a deceleration.

parts.title: Area under a speed–time graph = distance travelled
parts.html:
Because distance $=$ speed $\times$ time, the area between the line and the x-axis gives the distance travelled.

  • Under a horizontal line (constant speed) the shape is a rectangle: area $= \text{speed} \times \text{time}$.
  • Under a sloping line (accelerating from rest, or decelerating to rest) the shape is a triangle: area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{time} \times \text{speed}$.

Method: split the area into rectangles and triangles, work out each one, then add them up. Use the numbers on the axes, not centimetres on the paper.

parts.title: Acceleration and distance from a speed–time graph
parts.question: The graph shows a tram journey between two stops. Describe the journey, find the acceleration in the first 10 s, and find the total distance travelled.

graph.alt: Speed–time graph: up to 20 m/s in 10 s, constant to 30 s, down to 0 at 40 s, with the area split into two triangles and a rectangle

steps: Describe: 0–10 s constant acceleration from rest; 10–30 s constant speed of 20 m/s; 30–40 s constant deceleration to rest.
Acceleration in the first 10 s — gradient from $(0,\ 0)$ to $(10,\ 20)$:
Deceleration in the last 10 s: $\dfrac{0 - 20}{40 - 30} = \dfrac{-20}{10} = -2$ m/s², a deceleration of 2 m/s².

parts.title: Drawing a speed–time graph for a journey
parts.html:
1. Split the journey into stages and write down the time at the end of each stage and the speed at that moment.
  2. Plot each point and join them dot-to-dot with a ruler.
  3. Check: "constant speed" must be horizontal; "accelerates from rest" starts at speed 0; "comes to a stop" finishes at speed 0.

questions.text: A horizontal line appears on two different graphs.

parts.text: On a distance–time graph, a horizontal line means the object is…
parts.explain: Distance is not changing as time passes, so the object is stationary.
parts.label: a

parts.text: On a speed–time graph, a horizontal line above the axis means the object is…
parts.explain: Speed is not changing — but it is not zero, so the object is moving at a constant speed.
parts.label: b
